sentences.text: Together, our property tax moves raise $380 million more per year from a base of only 7% of all owner-occupied residential properties and all non-owner-occupied residential properties.

sections.label: Property tax revenue and rates
sections.summary: Property tax revenue from all residential properties is about $1 billion, and raising another $1 billion may require doubling rates across the board.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Currently, our total property tax revenue from all residential properties is about $1 billion.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: To raise another $1 billion from just property tax alone, property tax rates may very well need to be doubled across the board.

sections.label: Net wealth tax suggestion
sections.summary: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Louis Chua suggested a net wealth tax estimated to yield about $1.2 billion annually.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Louis Chua suggested we introduce a net wealth tax; and they estimated that it could yield about $1.2 billion annually.

sections.label: Household Support Package assistance
sections.summary: The Household Support Package will provide a household with two children up to $785 of assistance this year.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The Household Support Package will provide a household with two children up to $785 of assistance this year.

sections.label: Assurance Package and GST Voucher benefits
sections.summary: Over five years, they receive about $2,400 yearly in benefits, more than their total annual GST expenses of around $2,000.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Over the next five years, they will receive, on average, around $1,000 per year from the enhanced Assurance Package and around $1,400 per year from the enhanced GST Voucher – altogether, $2,400 per year of benefits over the next five years.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This is more than their annual total GST expenses – not the increase – more than their total annual GST expenses of around $2,000 per year over this same period.

sections.label: GST exemption revenue loss
sections.summary: Exempting four categories from GST would lose about $1.2 billion, with only $185 million benefiting the bottom 20% of resident households.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: If we were to exempt these four categories from GST, we expect to lose about $1.2 billion in tax revenue, of which only $185 million, or 15% of GST not collected, will benefit the bottom 20% of resident households.

sections.label: Single GST rate and vouchers
sections.summary: Studies by governments and the OECD support a single GST rate with direct help to lower- and middle-income Singaporean families through the GST Voucher scheme.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This conclusion has also been reached by studies by numerous governments as well as organisations like the OECD.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This is why, in fact, it is fairer and more effective for us to have a single GST rate across the board and to directly help lower-income and middle-income Singaporean families through the GST Voucher scheme, which is what we are doing.

sections.label: Bottom 10% GST offsets
sections.summary: Households in the bottom 10% pay no GST on average after offsets.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In fact, on average, the households at the bottom 10% do not pay any GST at all, after offsets.

sections.label: Effective GST rate unchanged
sections.summary: With the enhanced permanent GST Voucher scheme, the effective GST rate for the first three deciles remains unchanged.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Together with the enhanced permanent GST Voucher scheme, you can see from this chart, the effective GST rate for the first three deciles remains unchanged.

sections.label: Top 20% GST share
sections.summary: After the GST rate increase, the top 20% of citizen households pay a greater share of GST, rising from 40% to 42%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: After the GST rate increase, it is the top 20% of citizen households who will pay a greater share of GST and that is after GST Vouchers and the absorbed GST, netted off.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Top 20%, the share goes up from 40% to 42%.

sections.label: Retirees and household benefits
sections.summary: Retirees receive $6,900 in net benefits per person, and bottom decile employed households receive $5,900 per member, about 90% of household income.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Retirees, on average, receive $6,900 in net benefits per person.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Among Singaporean employed households, the benefits, net of taxes, are significant, at $5,900 per member for the bottom decile.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: When you add that up for a typical household, the benefits work out to be about 90% of their household income.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Put another way, Government benefits will nearly double the amount of resources for these households.

sections.label: Benefits per tax dollar
sections.summary: The bottom 20% receive about $4 in benefits per tax dollar, the middle 20% about $2, and the top 20% about $0.30.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The bottom 20% of Singaporean households receive about $4 in benefits for every tax dollar paid, the middle 20% of Singaporean households receive about $2 in benefits for every tax dollar paid and the top 20% of Singaporean households are net contributors receiving about $0.30 in benefits for every tax dollar paid.

sections.label: GST deferral and support
sections.summary: The GST was deferred to 2023 and staggered over two steps, while the Household Support Package doubles U-Save rebates and provides CDC vouchers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I understand the concerns that Singaporeans have about rising prices and the cost of living.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: That is precisely why I had decided to defer the GST to 2023 and to stagger the increase over two steps.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Meanwhile, we are extending significant help to Singaporeans through the Household Support Package – we will double the U-Save rebates this year for households, help them with their children’s education and also their daily essentials through the CDC vouchers.

sections.label: Family of four payouts
sections.summary: A family of four earning $2,500 in a 3-room HDB flat will receive around $2,400 a year over five years from the AP and GSTV.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: For example, a family of four earning $2,500, living in a 3-room HDB flat, will receive around $2,400 a year over the next five years from both the AP and GSTV.

sections.label: Tax changes fund healthcare
sections.summary: Budget tax changes on income and property make higher earners and owners of properties with annual value over $30,000 pay more, funding rising expenditures especially healthcare.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Besides the GST, we have also made other tax changes in this Budget, like the income and property taxes, so that those with higher incomes and who own properties with an annual value over $30,000 pay more taxes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: These tax changes will generate additional revenue which we urgently need to fund our rising Government expenditures, especially in the area of healthcare, so that we can take better care of our seniors.

sections.label: Drawing more from reserves
sections.summary: Some Members of Parliament have suggested drawing more from the reserves to cover the funding gap.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Some Members of Parliament have suggested that we should draw more from our reserves to cover our funding gap.

sections.label: Budget, donations and inflation
sections.summary: A man said paying more taxes is the right thing to do, a participant wanted to donate her Assurance Package payout, and an online portal will be set up for Singaporeans to indicate preferred charities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But his wife asked him: "Why are you so happy to pay more taxes?" His reply: "It's the right thing to do." In a dialogue organised by the CDCs, including their community and corporate partners, a participant said she did not need the cash payout from the Assurance Package and would like to donate it to families with greater needs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I was cheered by this and I am glad to share that we will have an online portal set up in the coming months, where Singaporeans can indicate their preferred charities for the Government to directly channel the payout to, if they wish.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In the end, the Budget is about all of us as Singaporeans, driven by our compassion and our conviction to build a better society for all; strengthening our trust in one another and keeping faith with future generations, as our forefathers kept faith with us.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And Sir, as one united people, we can be confident in charting our new way forward together and in building a fairer, greener and more inclusive Singapore together.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And we did so, of course, knowing that since the decision to raise GST was announced a few years ago, circumstances have changed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And core inflation right now is at its highest level in nine years.

sections.label: BEPS revenue impact estimates
sections.summary: The question asks for the Government's current estimates of the net impact of Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 on corporate income tax revenues, given the 2023 BEPS implementation deadline.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: To that end, my question is: can I ask what are the Government's current estimates, given that there is an implementation deadline of 2023 for BEPS?

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: What is the range of estimates of the net impact of Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 on our corporate income tax revenues?

sections.label: Hong Kong medium range forecast
sections.summary: Hong Kong has a medium range forecast right up to fiscal year 2026/2027.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Hong Kong has a medium range forecast right up to fiscal year 2026/2027.

sections.label: Healthcare resourcing review
sections.summary: The Minister said in his Budget speech that the Healthier SG strategy entails a review of resourcing, healthcare financing, upstream investments and preventive healthcare.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Minister himself recognised in his Budget speech that, I believe, there is a review of even healthcare resourcing at paragraph 239: "We are thinking through this healthier SG strategy carefully.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It will entail a review of our resourcing approach and healthcare financing schemes as well as the need for upstream investments and preventive healthcare." So, clearly, the other numbers that were in his speech about potentially where we could be with healthcare expenditure if we do not keep it in check, may not really be what will, eventually, be the outcome, because there is a review going on.

sections.label: Reserves draw and GST delay
sections.summary: The speaker cites a $42.9 billion draw on Past Reserves and says he decided to delay the GST and stagger the increase over two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: So, if you have some preamble, I would allow it, but please limit that time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: It was previously said that we have drawn on our reserves equivalent to 20 years of past Budget surpluses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: This was the Government position vis-a-vis COVID-19. "We have used a generation's worth of savings to combat a crisis of a generation." My colleague, Mr Louis Chua, asked Deputy Prime Minister Heng, in his capacity as Finance Minister previously, after accounting for the draw, where would our reserves be, compared to five years ago and 10 years ago?

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: After having a better fix on the number, $42.9 billion drawn on Past Reserves, where would our reserves be today, as compared to five years ago?

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I think that is a question that can be answered in one word.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: There are few of them and I will take them in turn.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: It was a very difficult decision for all the reasons I have explained: recognising, on the one hand, the concerns that Singaporeans have about higher prices but, on the other hand, the urgent and very pressing revenue needs we have to address.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: That is why I highlighted that I decided, eventually, to delay the GST and to stagger the increase over two years.

sections.label: Help delaying GST impact
sections.summary: A lot of help will, for most households, delay the impact of the GST increase by five years or more.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: A lot of help, which will, for most households, delay the impact of the GST increase by five years or more.

sections.label: NIRC share of GDP
sections.summary: NIRC is now about 3.5% of GDP on average over past years, and this is not expected to keep rising as a share of GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Whatever we are getting from NIRC today at 3.5% of GDP, on average, over the past few years, we do not expect that to continue rising as a share of GDP.

sections.label: BEPS 2.0 estimates considered
sections.summary: The speaker says they will consider whether to provide a range of estimates of BEPS 2.0's impact for Pillars 1 and 2.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, that is one of the reasons why I mentioned I hesitate to put out any figures at this stage.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But taking the earlier point about putting out more information for a more informed debate, we will go back and think about whether we might provide a range of estimates about what the impact of BEPS 2.0 might be for both Pillars 1 and 2.

sections.label: BEPS revenue and social spending
sections.summary: Even if Pillars 1 and 2 yield additional revenue, the speaker is not confident it will help social or healthcare spending needs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: What is more important, especially the point I mentioned, which is that even if Pillars 1 and 2, combined, yield us additional revenue, we will very likely have to reinvest that revenue back into ensuring we remain competitive and attract our fair share of investments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In fact, it will get even more intense, and it will intensify in other non-tax areas, which we will, therefore, have to fund and have resources ready for.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, even if there is a plus from BEPS 2.0, I am, in fact, not confident that that additional revenue will help us with our social spending needs, and, especially not for our healthcare spending needs, which will continue to rise very sharply.

sections.label: Top income tax versus GST
sections.summary: A 2 to 3 percentage point rise in the top personal income tax rate will not approach the revenue from a 2% GST increase.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: A 2-percentage point to 3-percentage point increase in the top personal income tax rate will never get anywhere close to the revenue we get from a 2% increase in GST.

sections.label: GST increase burden on top earners
sections.summary: The $3.5 billion from the 2% GST increase is borne by upper-middle and top income earners, per the effective rate chart.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Effectively, what it means is that the increase in GST, the $3.5 billion of revenues that the 2% of GST generates, will be borne by the upper-middle and the top income earners.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: It shows in the effective rate chart, where you saw, when we stacked up the effective GST rates and we showed the increase in GST to 9%, that extra burden is all borne by the upper-income deciles.

sections.label: Taxable income of top 10%
sections.summary: The question asks the Minister for the total taxable income attributable to the top 10%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Can I ask the Minister then, what is the total taxable income attributable to the top 10%?

sections.label: Short land leases and BEPS 2.0
sections.summary: It covers land leases of one to nine years and a commitment to implementing the spirit of BEPS 2.0.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: So, land leases that are of one to nine years, with the broad argument that land sales must all immediately go into reserves, rather than take the first nine years as part of recurrent revenue.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We are, certainly, committed to implementing the spirit of BEPS 2.0.

sections.label: Net wealth tax proposal
sections.summary: A proposal from Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and the Workers' Party for a net wealth tax yielding $1.2 billion is recognised.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: On wealth taxes, I recognise a proposal from Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and the Workers' Party for a net wealth tax that will yield revenue of $1.2 billion.

sections.label: Land sales revenue treatment
sections.summary: Shorter land leases are taken as current revenue, while longer leases are treated as assets in the reserves framework.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: On land sales, the easy answer is, for these shorter duration leases, we have decided for flexibility and, because there are more transactions like that, there is no need to regard them as assets and, therefore, we take them in as current revenue.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But for the ones with longer leases, we treat them as assets and then, therefore, we take them into our reserves framework and accord the treatment accordingly.

sections.label: Sin taxes not revenue
sections.summary: Sin and externality taxes are imposed for reasons other than generating revenue.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We look at the system as a whole.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And where sin taxes are concerned, externality tax, we do it not for revenue-generating purposes.

sections.label: GST and vouchers offset
sections.summary: GST is a broad-based consumption tax whose impact is offset by permanent GST Vouchers tied to the system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: It is a broad-based consumption tax which impacts everyone and everyone feels it, but it is also the way they can contribute and chip in to the system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But what we have done is do it in a fair way by offsetting the impact.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And because the GST Vouchers are permanent, they are conjoined with our GST system.

sections.label: Optimal reserves level
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister to agree that slowing reserve growth without depleting reserves is legitimate as reserves rise.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: The second clarification is on the concept of an optimal level of reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: I would invite the Minister to agree with me that as the absolute level of reserves increases in dollar terms as a proportion of GDP, we must accept that it is legitimate to bring into place policies that slow the growth of that reserve without depleting it.

sections.label: Alternative groups to tax
sections.summary: The proposal is to tax more from the wealthy, large companies and future generations instead of GST.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Basically, you are asking to tax more from three possible groups as an alternative to GST: the wealthy and the better-off, large companies and future generations.

sections.label: Wealth, property, income taxes
sections.summary: Wealth taxes are difficult, and getting another billion from property tax would likely require doubling rates.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And that means wealth taxes, which, I have explained, can be difficult to do, or property tax or personal income tax.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And, if you were to home in on property tax, I have explained, if you want to get another billion dollars of revenue from property tax, you probably would have to double property tax rates across the board.

sections.label: Budget cuts are real
sections.summary: Budget cuts are real and applied to Ministry expenditures within a budgetary framework.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: When we talk about these Budget cuts, they are in the context of a budgetary framework that allows us to reduce – so, the cuts are real, mind you.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The cuts are real and actually applied to Ministry expenditures.

sections.label: Recording of dissent
sections.summary: A record of the dissent is being taken.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: Mr Leong, we are taking a record of the dissent.

sections.label: Dissent recorded in person
sections.summary: They take the same position but must be in person to record their dissent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I just want to state that they take the same position as well.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: But they need to be in person to record their dissent.

sections.label: Concerns over GST increase
sections.summary: They disagree with raising the Goods and Services Tax now, and Workers' Party MPs will offer alternative revenue ideas.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, there are aspects of the Budget that are of concern to us.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We disagree with the decision to raise the Goods and Services Tax, especially at this time, and the Workers' Party Members of Parliament who speak after me will put forward alternative ideas for revenue generation.

sections.label: Workers' Party on GST
sections.summary: The Workers' Party's position is that the Government need not raise the GST.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Workers' Party's position is that the Government need not raise the GST.

sections.label: Reserves framework proposals
sections.summary: The Workers' Party proposed including a portion of land sales in recurrent revenue and raising the NIRC for recurrent spending to 60% from 50%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Workers' Party has also previously asked if we can tweak the reserves framework and the way reserves contribute to our Budget.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We have proposed including a portion of land sales into recurrent revenue and also an adjustment of the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) allowed for recurrent spending to be raised to 60% from the current 50%.

sections.label: Projected healthcare spending
sections.summary: The Minister projected yearly healthcare spending could reach $27 billion by 2030, compared to $11.3 billion in 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Minister projected that, starting from current levels of healthcare spending and assuming increases at a similar rate in the next 10 years, the Government could be spending $27 billion on healthcare yearly by 2030, compared to $11.3 billion in 2019.

sections.label: NIRC budget revenue changes
sections.summary: The 2008 NIR change and 2015 Temasek inclusion made NIRC the largest yearly Budget revenue source, rising from about $2 billion in 2006 to close to $22 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The 2008 change of the Net Investment Income to Net Investment Returns (NIR) with the immediate conclusion of up to 50% of NIR contributions from MAS and GIC and the inclusion of Temasek in the NIRC formula in 2015 were all deliberate moves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: These changes have made the NIRC component the largest source of revenue for the yearly Budget from around $2 billion in 2006 to close to $22 billion for the upcoming financial year.

sections.label: MOF medium-term budget forecasting
sections.summary: The passage asks the Minister why MOF does not make medium-term forecasting part of the public-facing budgetary process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Can the Minister tell us why MOF does not make such medium-term forecasting a part of our public-facing budgetary process?

sections.label: GST offsets and price rises
sections.summary: If price rises aggregate significantly, additional offsets may not offset the GST hike as optimistically as Annex F-2 estimates for 3-room and 4-room HDB households.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Should the aggregate of price rises be significant, the impact of the additional offsets may not be as optimistic as highlighted in Annex F–2 of the Budget Statement for 3-room and 4-room HDB households where the enhanced Assurance Package is estimated to offset the GST hike of 11.8 and 7.9 years respectively.

sections.label: CPI utilities and transport
sections.summary: Last month's CPI data show utilities and other fuels rose 11.8% and transport 12.7% year-on-year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: CPI data from last month show that utilities and other fuels rose 11.8% compared to a year earlier and transport is up 12.7% year-on-year.

sections.label: Adult card fare changes
sections.summary: Adult card fares alternated up and down between 2014 and 2017, then rose six cents in 2018, nine cents in 2019 and three to four cents in 2020.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: While adult card fares were alternatingly increased and reduced between 2014 and 2017, they were raised by six cents in 2018, a further nine cents in 2019 and then another three to four cents in 2020.

sections.label: PWM Credit Scheme wage uplift
sections.summary: The passage asks the Minister for Finance to consider using the PWM Credit Scheme to immediately raise wages of workers taking home under $1,300.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In this regard, I hope the Minister for Finance can consider moving more decisively to ensure that Singaporean workers who take home less than $1,300 can rely on the PWM Credit Scheme to raise their wages immediately.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Assuming that we want to provide immediate relief to the 32,000 full-time Singaporean workers who earn less than $1,300 with a generous $400 a month wage hike for 13 months each financial year, a back-of-the-envelope calculation shows that it would require about $167 million year to significantly uplift the well-being of these lower-income workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This sum would constitute 8% of the $2 billion set aside under the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) Credit Scheme and only 9.2% of the $1.8 billion that the Government has committed each year over the next five years for this scheme.

sections.label: Minimum income criterion introduced
sections.summary: The Finance Minister introduced a new minimum income criterion of $500 a month.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Finance Minister has introduced a new minimum income criterion of $500 a month.

sections.label: Workfare denied to low earners
sections.summary: 46,600 residents earned under $500 a month last year, and the new criterion will deny them Workfare Income Supplement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: According to the MOM Labour Force, Singapore 2021 data set, there were 46,600 residents who earned less than $500 a month last year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The new criterion will deny the work for Workfare Income Supplement to these workers.

sections.label: Carbon tax by 2030
sections.summary: The Budget announced a carbon tax of $50 to $80 per tonne of emissions by 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Budget announcement of a carbon tax of $50 to $80 per tonne of emissions by 2030 is consistent with a commitment to mitigate the climate emergency.

sections.label: S Pass salary and ITM tracking
sections.summary: S Pass minimum qualifying salary rises from $2,500 to $3,000, and the ITM framework should track reliance on S Pass holders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: With the minimum qualifying salary for new S Pass holders increasing from $2,500 to $3,000 this September and further increases already forecasted for September 2024 and 2025, it would be useful for the ITM framework to proactively track, disclose and identify which are the ITM sectors are more reliant on S Pass holders and where there could be opportunities for Singaporean workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The same expectation should be set aside for the large taxpayers' dollars set aside for national plans like the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2025 Plan where $25 billion has been allocated from 2021 to 2025.

sections.label: Workers' Party objects to GST
sections.summary: The Workers' Party notes the Budget's thrust but will object because it disagrees with raising the GST.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Workers' Party notes the broad thrust of the Budget and supports the call of greater fairness, sustainability and a more inclusive society, a philosophy that comes with much promise of the future.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, the Workers' Party will object to the Budget as we disagree with the decision to raise the GST.

sections.label: Ukraine impact on Budget
sections.summary: The Finance Minister is asked whether the Ukraine situation affects the 18 February Budget and the economy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Can I ask the Finance Minister for an update, notwithstanding the Foreign Affairs Minister's Statement, as to whether the Ukraine situation will have a bearing on the Budget that he delivered on 18 February; and also, what other implication or impact will there be for our economy?

sections.label: Budget tax increases revenue
sections.summary: Budget income tax and wealth tax increases raise an additional $600 million, a small sum given their narrow base.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: In the Budget, we saw significant increases in the income tax rate as well as the wealth taxes: property tax, luxuries car taxes in the ARF.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: These increases will bring in an additional revenue of $600 million for the Government, not quite a needle-moving number that can pay for the projected rise in expenditure due to its narrow base.

sections.label: Assurance Package GST cushion
sections.summary: A $6.6 billion upsized Assurance Package accompanies the GST increase to cushion its impact.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Coupled with this increase will be the massive upsized $6.6 billion Assurance Package to cushion the impact of the GST increase.

sections.label: Progressive Wage Model expansion
sections.summary: Budget expands the Progressive Wage Model, co-funding firms and requiring local qualifying salaries, worth about $1.8 billion yearly over five years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: In this Budget, we saw significant expansions to the Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: It will be extended to more sectors with an aim to cover 94% of our full-time lower-wage workers and through an accelerated pace of implementation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Businesses with workers earning up to $2,500 per month will be assisted with co-funding of 50% in the first two years and 30% in the next two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: In a related move, companies who employ foreign workers will now be required to pay all their local employees at least the local qualifying salary of $1,400 per month.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: The qualifying income gap will be increased to $2,500 and also extending to younger workers, aged 30, as well as increased payouts amongst the various WIS enhancements.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: These various measures amounted to a very substantial package to uplift the wages of the lower-income workers about $1.8 billion per year over the next five years or totalling $9 billion for both PWCS and enhanced Workfare.

sections.label: Carbon tax increases
sections.summary: Carbon tax rises five-fold from $5 to $25 per tonne in 2024, and ten-fold or more by around 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: The announced carbon tax increases are steep, increasing five-folds, from $5 to $25 per tonne in 2024 and thereafter, by ten-folds and more by around 2030.

sections.label: Assistance versus GST paid
sections.summary: A 3-room flat family with two children receives nearly $5,000 in Assurance Package assistance but pays about $400 more GST.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: For example, a family living in a 3-room flat with two children will receive nearly $5,000 worth of assistance from this Assurance Package, but roughly, this family will only have to pay an additional $400 GST.

sections.label: Utilities rebates by flat size
sections.summary: Utilities rebates give 1-room and 2-room households up to eight to 10 months, 3-room and 4-room four to six months, and 5-room three months.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: For utilities, 1-room and 2-room households will receive rebates of up to eight to 10 months, 3-room and 4-room households will receive rebates of up to four to six months, and 5-room households will receive rebates of three months.

sections.label: GST burden and subsidies
sections.summary: MOF figures show 60% of GST comes from high-income earners and tourists, and low-income earners get a $4 subsidy per $1 of tax.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: According to MOF figures, 60% of the GST collected come from high-income earners and tourists.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Under our overall tax and grant system, low-income earners will receive a $4 subsidy for every $1 of tax paid.

sections.label: GST rate hike delay
sections.summary: The GST rate hike will be delayed and spread over two steps of one percentage point each on 1 January 2023 and 1 January 2024.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: One of the main Budget announcements was that the GST rate hike will be delayed and spread out over two steps – one-percentage point per step on 1 January 2023 and another one on 1 January 2024.

sections.label: Taxes on the wealthy
sections.summary: Taxes on the wealthy, including personal income tax, property tax and luxury car tax, are expected to raise $600 million yearly.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: It unveiled a slew of taxes that impacts the wealthy – ranging from personal income tax, property tax as well as luxury car tax.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: These taxes are expected to raise $600 million of additional tax revenue per year when implemented.

sections.label: Stamp Duty collection increase
sections.summary: In 2021, Stamp Duty collection rose to $6.45 billion, a $2.55 billion or 66% increase from 2020.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: In 2021, Stamp Duty collection increased to $6.45 billion, that means a $2.55 billion increase in one year as compared to 2020, and that is 66% increase in one year.

sections.label: Assurance Package boost
sections.summary: The Assurance Package, designed to cushion GST impact for middle- and low-income households, was boosted to $6.6 billion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: In this Budget, the Assurance Package – designed to cushion GST impact for middle- and low-income households, was boosted to $6.6 billion.

sections.label: Carbon tax increase
sections.summary: The carbon tax will be raised progressively to $50 to $80 per tonne of emissions by 2030.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: To achieve this, the carbon tax will be raised progressively to $50 to $80 per tonne of emissions by 2030, higher, much higher than many had expected.

sections.label: Employment pass salary increases
sections.summary: Planned increases in qualifying salaries for employment pass and S Pass holders take effect from September and will hurt.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: The planned increases in qualifying salaries for employment pass and S Pass holders, which will take effect from September, will hurt.

sections.label: Core inflation and oil prices
sections.summary: Core inflation reached 2.4% in January and may exceed 3% in the second quarter as crude oil prices soar past US$100.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: After reaching a near-decade high of 2.4% in January, Singapore's core inflation is anticipated to possibly exceed 3% and above in the second quarter.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: With the Russia-Ukraine crisis, crude oil prices have been soaring and hitting over US$100 today.

sections.label: Budget 2022 integral development approach
sections.summary: Budget 2022 takes an integral development approach, and a National Business Study shows fewer businesses negatively impacted by COVID-19 and growing optimism.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Whether it is the $500 million Jobs and Business Support, or the timing of the GST rate hikes; whether it is the carbon tax increase to signal the urgent action for de-carbonisation, or the R&D budget for the Singapore Green Plan 2030; whether it is the investment in new capabilities of our people and our local enterprises, or the rollout of the Assurance Package and the uplifting low-wage workers with Progressive Wage Model implementation, it is a Budget that has taken an integral development approach to ensure that our people, our environment and our economy progress in tandem and in harmony.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the latest National Business Study conducted by SBF, businesses that reported being negatively impacted by COVID-19 declined from 63% in 2020 to 32%.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: There is growing optimism as eight in 10 firms are confident about sustaining their operations in 2022, compared to seven in 10 firms in the previous survey.

sections.label: Business support in Budget 2022
sections.summary: Budget 2022 covers business support areas including deferred GST hike, capability investment, openness to global talent, and Singapore Green Plan 2030 measures.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Budget 2022 does cover many of the areas that the businesses have called out for Government support: (a) everyone is relieved to hear Minister Lawrence Wong announce deferring and staging GST rate hike implementation; (b) the continued support for businesses to invest in new capabilities like digitalisation and automation is very much welcomed by the business community but the escalating costs of IT manpower and the shortage of IT skills continue to be a challenge; (c) Singapore being open to the best global talents to complement our local workforce gets the thumbs-up by both local business leaders and leaders of MNCs, though they still worry about policies not being aligned to the goal; and (d) a Budget carrying both the stick and the carrot to rally our businesses into action toward achieving our Singapore Green Plan 2030 is acknowledged as inevitable and that there is a lot of work ahead of all of us.

sections.label: Industries facing labour shortage
sections.summary: Industries hit by labour shortage exacerbated by border restrictions saw companies join WSG recruitment fairs with little success hiring Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: These industries have been hit hard with labour shortage, exacerbated by border restrictions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: And many companies in these industries have participated actively in WSG-organised recruitment fairs over the past two years in an attempt to hire more Singaporeans to fill the open positions but have had little success.

sections.label: Local Enterprises Funding Platform
sections.summary: Last year during the Committee of Supply, the speaker applauded the $1 billion Local Enterprises Funding Platform set up by Temasek and the Government.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Last year during the Committee of Supply, I applauded the $1 billion "Local Enterprises Funding Platform" set up by Temasek and the Government.

sections.label: SMEs, EFS, public service scholars
sections.summary: SMEs welcome enhanced EFS for Merger and Acquisition and Trade Loans, and a suggestion is made to assign Public Service scholars to SMEs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It would be interesting to see how many of such cases did happen.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: That said, the SMEs do welcome the announcement that Minister Lawrence Wong made in this year's Budget that EFS will be enhanced to include Merger and Acquisition and Trade Loans.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Talent is a big topic and a big challenge.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I will focus today on one small suggestion: that is, getting our cohort of Public Service scholars to get their feet wet and their hands dirty by being assigned to our promising SMEs for a year or two, or even six months, as part of their bond.

sections.label: INC course feedback and cohort
sections.summary: Feedback has been positive, with 41% of the first graduating cohort offered jobs, and the second INC cohort doubled in size.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The feedback has been very positive and to-date, 41% of the first cohort graduating May this year are already offered jobs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: With the positive feedback on the course, the second cohort of students undergoing INC have doubled in size.

sections.label: Advanced Manufacturing Learning Journey participation
sections.summary: Since October 2020, 177 companies and 632 professionals joined the Advanced Manufacturing Learning Journey, with over 20 companies developing projects with SP.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Since the launch in October 2020, 177 companies and 632 professionals have gone through the "Advanced Manufacturing Learning Journey".

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: More than 20 companies have taken the next step to work with SP to assess where they are and have gone on to develop projects with SP staff, some involving SP final Students as part of their Final Year Projects (FYPs), while others have SP students working projects as part of their internships.

sections.label: Minister Wong on economy
sections.summary: Minister Wong painted a cautiously optimistic picture of Singapore's and the global economy, with 7.6% growth last year exceeding MTI's forecast.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Minister Wong began his speech by painting a cautiously optimistic picture of both Singapore's as well as the global economy.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We grew by 7.6% last year, exceeding even the upper bound of MTI's forecast.

sections.label: January inflation at 4%
sections.summary: In January, inflation was 4% compared to a year ago, the highest in almost a decade.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In January, inflation clocked in at 4% compared to prices a year ago and the highest prices in almost a decade.

sections.label: IMF world GDP forecast
sections.summary: The IMF forecasts world GDP growth slowing from 4.4% this year to 2% in 2023 and 1.6% in 2024.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The International Monetary Fund forecasts a slowing of world GDP growth from an anticipated 4.4% this year, to just 2% in 2023 and 1.6% in 2024.

sections.label: MAS inflation forecast raised
sections.summary: MAS raised its latest inflation forecast to the 2.5% to 3.5% range.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Indeed, MAS expects as much, having raised its latest forecast of inflation to the 2.5% to 3.5% range.

sections.label: GST flat tax regressivity
sections.summary: GST is a flat tax on all purchases of goods and services, hitting lower-income households disproportionately more.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The GST is a flat tax rate applied to all purchases of goods and services, which hits lower-income households disproportionately more.

sections.label: GST increase and progressivity
sections.summary: A GST increase would reduce progressivity, and the Ministry is asked to clarify whether raising GST with an expanded GSTV scheme is net more or less progressive.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: But an increase in GST will, in and of itself, reduce progressivity, which means we end up less progressive than compared to the status quo.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I, therefore, welcome the Ministry to clarify if the plan to raise GST while expanding the scope of the permanent GST Voucher (GSTV) scheme would be net for the nation as a whole be more or less progressive, relative to a scenario of not increasing GST at all.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This is because we all understand that the generous $6.6 billion Assurance Package, while certainly welcome during the transitional period, will not last forever.

sections.label: GSTV income threshold exclusion
sections.summary: The GSTV income threshold excludes those above the 40% percentile of earners, so those earning over around $2,800 a month face the full GST increase after the transition period.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Income threshold for qualifying for GSTV will exclude those above the 40% percentile of earners.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This means that those earning more than around $2,800 a month – a decent but hardly comfortable salary – will face the full force of the GST increase once the transition period concludes.

sections.label: Workers' Party alternative revenue levers
sections.summary: Workers' Party colleagues worked out additional levers whose revenue possibilities could amount to close to the $3.6 billion expected from a GST hike.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: My colleagues at the Workers' Party have in the spirit of providing credible alternatives work out several additional levers, where if deployed, could stave off the need to increase GST.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We have worked out the revenue possibilities for each of these levers which could amount to close to the $3.6 billion expected in revenue from a GST hike.

sections.label: Reserves and corporate tax levers
sections.summary: Reduced reserve accumulation could generate $4.31 billion, and limiting increases to no more than 28% would allow raising the effective corporate tax rate to 8%, generating $3.65 billion.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The level of reserves will not go down, but merely represents a reduction in the rate of accumulation of reserves and this alone could generate $4.31 billion.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We limit the increases in each of these channels to no more than 28%, which is what the GST increase will entail.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: And these additional increases will then allow us to increase the effective corporate tax rate to just 8% and this would generate $3.65 billion.

sections.label: Alternatives to raising GST
sections.summary: The passage states that adjusting levers could allow choosing not to raise GST, with each lever sufficient to meet revenue needs.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: First, it is to put on the table the tantalising possibility that we can, in fact, choose not to raise GST by adjusting some of the levers available to us.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We have deliberately worked out the math behind each of these alternatives such that any single one of these levers will be sufficient to meet the revenue needs that raising GST will offer.

sections.label: Heng out of running
sections.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Heng took himself out of the running, citing several reasons.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng had taken himself out of the running citing several reasons.

sections.label: Reasons for longer runway
sections.summary: The Deputy Prime Minister said the next Prime Minister should have a longer runway and a long run in the premiership.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In short, the Deputy Prime Minister said the next Prime Minister should have a longer runway to the premiership and a long run in the premiership.

sections.label: Long-term leadership succession plan
sections.summary: Singapore must have a long-term leadership succession plan to make long-term plans like this year's Budget work.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: To make Singapore's long-term plans work, such as those contained in this year's Budget, Singapore must have a long-term leadership succession plan.

sections.label: PAP renewal and concretising plans
sections.summary: The passage says renewal is key and plans for it need to be concretised, recounting how the PAP transformed and renewed itself.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Of ensuring that tomorrow will be better than today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: This book recounts how the PAP continuously transformed and renewed itself over the decades." So, renewal is key, Sir, and we need to concretise the plans for it.

sections.label: Choosing best-fit team leader
sections.summary: The passage states the 4G can choose someone not necessarily the smartest but the best fit to bring together a team.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The point I am making is that you, the 4G, can choose someone who is not necessarily the smartest, but you need to choose someone who is the best fit to bring together a team.

sections.label: Parliament showing succession plan
sections.summary: The speaker says Parliament should show the world it can sort out its succession plan during the pandemic.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The point I am making here, and the point behind this speech is: for us in Parliament to show the world that, in the middle of this pandemic, we can even sort out the succession plan.

sections.label: Lining up future leaders
sections.summary: The speaker says solid leadership exists now but the future Prime Minister and deputies must be lined up urgently.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The point I am making is that we have solid leadership now, but we must, with utmost imperative, line up the future Prime Minister and his or her deputies, so that they get the longest runway possible before taking over the controls in the cockpit.

sections.label: PAP choosing next leaders
sections.summary: The speaker proposes that the PAP swiftly choose the next Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Ministers and give them a long runway.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Along with PAP's effort, coupled with the sweat of Singaporeans, Singapore has transitioned from third world to first and become a choice destination to invest in the 2020s.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: It is with this belief and principle in mind that I make the propositions today, that is, the ruling party of the day – the PAP, must swiftly choose the next Prime Minister and next Deputy Prime Ministers and give them as long a runway as our current Prime Minister can manage.

sections.label: Entry years of leaders
sections.summary: The speaker says he entered in 2006 at age 30 at the Prime Minister's request, and many 4G Prime Minister candidates entered in 2011 and 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: He has no need to mince his words.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: I entered in 2006 at the age of 30, at the request of the Prime Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Many of the candidates for the 4G Prime Minister entered in 2011 and 2015.

sections.label: Message to 4G on succession
sections.summary: The speaker urges the 4G to apply their minds to succession planning and articulate their leadership choice to Singaporeans swiftly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: My humble message to the 4G is this: please apply your minds to succession planning and articulate swiftly your thinking and choice as regards to the leadership to Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In the throes of a crisis, we can pick a future leader and the core team to take Singapore through its next chapter and beyond.

sections.label: Chamber seen as ivory tower
sections.summary: The speaker says it is highly concerning that people perceive this Chamber as an ivory tower out of touch with reality.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The situation where our people feel and perceive that this Chamber is an ivory tower that is out of touch with reality is highly concerning and one which cannot be allowed to carry on.

sections.label: Hardship of seniors and parents
sections.summary: The passage asks what it says about society that seniors cut medication dosages and parents cannot afford nappies and formula.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: After all, what does it say about us as a society that our senior residents come to us and tell us as a matter of course that they have requested for their medication dosages to be cut down because they cannot afford to pay for the full dosages that doctors have prescribed to them to treat their medical ailments?

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: What does it say about us when our young parents have to make daily choices about how to apply the last dollars in their bank accounts as they cannot afford to buy both nappies and formula for their newborns, when the family is hit by an unexpected job loss through no fault of their own?

sections.label: UK fit notes rule
sections.summary: In the UK, employers may only ask for fit notes if employees are sick for more than seven days.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Indeed, in the UK, employers are only allowed to ask for "fit notes" if employees are sick for more than seven days.

sections.label: Price increases and tax rise
sections.summary: Individuals, households and businesses report price increases, a 2% tax rise meaning 28% more tax, and a coffeeshop raising prices 50 cents.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Individuals, households and businesses have approached us for assistance with juggling the impact of relentless price increases.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: They have noted that a final 2% tax increase means a 28% increase in the amount of tax to be paid.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Just the other day, I noted during one of my estate walks that a Buangkok coffeeshop stall has put up a sign stating that rising prices have obliged them to increase the price of all items by 50 cents, which definitely far exceeds 2%.

sections.label: Crude oil and stock markets
sections.summary: Crude oil has hit multi-year highs of over $100 a barrel and stock markets have reacted with volatility.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Already, crude oil has hit multi-year highs of over $100 a barrel and stock markets have reacted with volatility.

sections.label: Workers' Party opposes GST hike
sections.summary: The passage says green transformation is urgent and the Workers' Party cannot agree to a GST hike as alternatives are not exhausted.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: All these further underscores the need for our green transformation to take place urgently.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It is why the Workers' Party cannot agree to a GST hike – whether delayed or staggered – especially as we believe not all other alternatives have been exhausted.

sections.label: Exempting essential items from GST
sections.summary: The passage argues that exempting key essential items from GST will significantly reduce the impact on lower-income groups.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: While it is true that exempting essential items from GST is regressive, the alternative of keeping our existing system of no exemptions is likely to be even more regressive.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This is because those who are on a lower income spend a far larger proportion of their income on consumption, which is always taxed in our case.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Therefore, exempting key essential items from being taxed will significantly reduce the impact on lower-income groups.

sections.label: Singapore dashboard beyond GDP
sections.summary: A uniquely Singapore dashboard should be developed and published with GDP results, measuring poverty reduction, social mobility and wealth distribution.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: A uniquely Singapore dashboard should, therefore, be developed and published together with GDP results.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This can contain quarterly or annual measurements of our progress in terms of poverty reduction, social mobility and wealth distribution in an easy-to-understand way, allowing us as a people to understand at a glance what our targets are and the progress we have made or failed to make beyond GDP figures.

sections.label: Impact dashboard environmental indices
sections.summary: The impact dashboard could contain indices on emissions, land use changes and waste reduction, with measures on the green economy transition.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Our impact dashboard could, for example, contain indices relating to our emissions, land use changes, waste reduction efforts and have specific measures on how well we are doing in our transition to a green economy – a topic that my colleague Dennis Tan will elaborate more on.

sections.label: Voting no to GST increase
sections.summary: The speaker says the difficult environment should not be worsened by raising GST, so they must vote no and cannot support the Budget.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The difficult environment we see ahead of us will test us and we should not add further to the financial and other burdens of our people by raising our GST when there are other available options.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It is therefore regrettable that we must vote no to a GST increase and therefore cannot support this Budget.

sections.label: Net-zero emissions by 2050
sections.summary: The Budget outlines an ambition to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: The ambition, as outlined in the Budget, is to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.

sections.label: Carbon services gross value added
sections.summary: Economic opportunities from carbon services could create projected gross value added of between US$1.8 billion and US$5.6 billion in Singapore by 2050.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: The estimates are that economic opportunities from carbon services could create a projected gross value added (GVA) of between US$1.8 billion to US$5.6 billion in Singapore by 2050.

sections.label: Digital capabilities and worker support
sections.summary: An additional $200 million will fund enhanced digital capability schemes, but support for companies to help workers gain knowledge and skills is also needed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: While there will be an additional $200 million to fund enhanced schemes to build digital capabilities in our businesses and workers, I think we also need to look at what support will be given to companies to help workers, especially those in the workforce gain the knowledge and skills they need in this new world of work.

sections.label: Assurance Package GST cushioning
sections.summary: The Assurance Package provides more for lower-income households and signals intent to cushion the GST increase for more middle-income households.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: While the support in the Assurance Package should and does provide more for the lower-income, the Assurance Package does also signal the Government's intent to also cushion the impact of the GST increase to include more middle-income households.

sections.label: COVID-19 Support Grant eligibility
sections.summary: Job losers meeting CSG criteria but living in homes with AV above $21,000, regardless of ownership, are not eligible for the COVID-19 Support Grant.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: An example is the COVID-19 Support Grant (CSG).

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: Those who have lost their jobs and meet the CSG eligibility criteria, but live in a home of AV above $21,000, regardless of ownership, are not eligible for the COVID-19 Support Grant.

sections.label: WIS income cap and criterion
sections.summary: The qualifying income cap rises from $2,300 to $2,500 and extends to workers aged 30 to 34, with higher payouts per tier, but the $500 minimum income criterion is questioned.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: The rise in qualifying income cap from $2,300 to $2,500, and the extension to younger workers aged 30 to 34 will definitely benefit workers and the increased payouts for each tier will provide more support for lower-wage workers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: I do, however, want to appeal to Minister Wong to reconsider the introduction of the minimum income criterion of $500 per month.

sections.label: Review of WIS minimum income
sections.summary: A review of the minimum income criterion for WIS is requested because it will impact those the scheme is intended to support.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: Will Minister consider a review of the minimum income criterion for WIS, as it will impact those that the scheme is intended to support.

sections.label: Support for Budget 2022
sections.summary: Budget 2022 aims to chart the way forward, realise a fairer, more sustainable, more inclusive society, see through the pandemic and build a better Singapore tomorrow.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: Budget 2022 sets out to "charting our way forward" I thank Minister Wong for a Budget the aims to "realising our vision of a fairer, more sustainable, and more inclusive society", to "see through the pandemic today" and more importantly, "to build a better Singapore tomorrow." I support the Budget.

sections.label: Singapore electricity from natural gas
sections.summary: About 95% of Singapore's electricity is generated using natural gas, based on public domain data.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Today, from public domain data, about 95% of Singapore's electricity is generated using natural gas.

sections.label: Diversifying Singapore electricity sources
sections.summary: The passage argues Singapore should diversify electricity sources ahead of the market for energy resilience, security and lower carbon footprint.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: But if the pandemic has taught us one thing, it is that we need to move from "just in time" to "just in case".

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: There is a case for Singapore to further diversify our electricity sources and to do so ahead of the market – for energy resilience, energy security, also to reduce our carbon footprint as part of the climate crisis response.

sections.label: Hydrogen shipping and Australia
sections.summary: Reuters reported a Japanese-Australian venture testing hydrogen shipping and a first liquefied hydrogen cargo from Australia to Japan; CSIS assessed Australia could be a major hydrogen player by 2030.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Reuters News Agency recently reported that a Japanese-Australian venture has been testing transport of hydrogen, using a ship as a liquid hydrogen carrier.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: They reported that just this past week, a Japanese-built ship, the Suiso Frontier, delivered the world's first long-distance liquefied hydrogen cargo from Australia to Japan.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: American think-tank, CSIS, in October 2021, published a commentary.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: They assess that Australia, by 2030, could well be a "major player" in global hydrogen production and trade.

sections.label: Nuclear power and fusion energy
sections.summary: The IEA observed nuclear power avoided about 55 gigatonnes of carbon emissions over 50 years, and a JET team generated 59 megajoules in five seconds.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: The International Energy Agency (IEA) in 2021 observed that nuclear power output avoided about 55 gigatonnes – 55 billion tonnes – of carbon emissions over the past 50 years, nearly equal to two years of global energy-related CO2 emissions.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: For nuclear fission, we should continue assessing the safety of small modular reactors and whether a future generation of small modular reactors can be safely deployed in the Singapore context.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: In December 2021, a team at the Joint European Torus (JET) facility near Oxford generated 59 megajoules of energy for five seconds – enough energy to power 35,000 homes for those five seconds.

sections.label: New energy capabilities needed
sections.summary: The passage states the climate crisis and climate ambition require new capabilities for energy security and decarbonisation.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: What do we need to do, that we cannot yet do?" Sir, the climate crisis and our climate ambition means we need new capabilities for our energy security and our decarbonisation.

sections.label: Singapore GDP and employment growth
sections.summary: Singapore's GDP grew 7.6% in 2021, with 3% to 5% growth projected for 2022 and total employment rising 47,400 workers in the fourth quarter.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Singapore's GDP grew by 7.6% in 2021, with the Government projecting an above-trend 3% to 5% growth for 2022, with total employment seeing the highest quarterly growth – since 2014 – of 47,400 workers in the fourth quarter.

sections.label: Property tax and wealth tax revenues
sections.summary: Higher property taxes and ARF are expected to raise annual revenues by $430 million, with total increases about $600 million including personal income tax changes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Higher property taxes and ARF are expected to result in a $430 million increase in annual revenues and, even if we include higher personal income tax rates, the total annual increase is just about $600 million.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: For example, in a November 2021 CNA article, Assoc Prof Walter Theseira from SUSS noted that a wealth tax might conceivably pull in a similar amount to raising the GST by a few percentage points, while a Bloomberg article on 16 February quoted Mr Christopher Gee, Senior Research Fellow at the IPS, as sharing that a similar wealth tax rate in Singapore, as that of Switzerland presumably, would generate $2.7 billion in Government revenues.

sections.label: Property tax increase examples
sections.summary: An owner-occupied central condominium is expected to see a $200 yearly increase while a very large landed property sees a $15,400 increase.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: As noted in Annex C-2 of the Budget Statement, an owner-occupied condominium in a central location is only expected to see an increase of $200 a year while a very large, landed property is expected to see a $15,400 increase.

sections.label: Personal income tax increases
sections.summary: Someone making $1 million pays $5,000 more, and someone making $1.5 million pays $15,000 more in personal income taxes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: For example, someone making $1 million in chargeable income would pay a grand total of $5,000 more in personal income taxes, or 0.5% of chargeable income, while someone making $1.5 million would only pay $15,000 more, or about 1% of chargeable income.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I would even argue that the last increase in personal income tax rates in Budget 2015, where the top marginal personal income tax rates were raised to 22% among others, was an even bolder move than what we have today, raising more revenues at $400 million a year back then, as compared to $117 million a year, with today's change.

sections.label: Singapore tax features
sections.summary: Singapore has no capital gains tax, no tax on dividends, no inheritance tax, no estate duties and low effective personal income tax rates.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Singapore will fit into both of these cases as a country with no capital gains tax, no tax on dividends, no inheritance tax, no estate duties and still has one of the lowest effective personal income tax rates globally.

sections.label: CIT revenue growth
sections.summary: Revised FY2021 CIT revenues are expected to exceed FY2019 levels at $17.5 billion, growing 9% year-on-year or $1.4 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Revised FY2021 CIT revenues are expected to exceed FY2019 levels at $17.5 billion, growing by 9% year-on-year or $1.4 billion, and this is expected to continue into FY2022, reaching a new high of $18.2 billion.

sections.label: Global minimum tax impact
sections.summary: The question asks for the Government's estimates of the net impact of pillar one and pillar two on CIT revenues.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: With less than a year to go before the implementation of the two-pillar solution and with OECD already having published in December last year the model rules for domestic implementation of the 15% global minimum tax, my question is, what is the Government's current estimates or range of estimates of the net impact of pillar one and pillar two to our CIT revenues?

sections.label: Hypothetical 15% tax rate
sections.summary: Assuming a 15% tax rate instead, this could hypothetically balloon seven times to $71.5 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: If we assume a 15% tax rate instead, this could hypothetically balloon seven times to $71.5 billion.

sections.label: Reserves draw and NIRC
sections.summary: Actual reserves used over three years was $43 billion, saving about $11 billion against the $54 billion announced in Budget 2021.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Lastly, let me touch on the other elephants in the room, the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) and our reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It is comforting to note that instead of a $54 billion draw on the reserves, as announced in Budget 2021, the actual amount we utilised across three years was $43 billion, savings of about $11 billion.

sections.label: MAS Official Foreign Reserves
sections.summary: MAS Official Foreign Reserves stand at around $566 billion as of January 2022, up $185 billion or close to 50% from two years ago.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It is not that I disagree with the need to be prudent and I agree we should not take our reserves for granted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: But just looking at the MAS Official Foreign Reserves (OFR), they stand at around $566 billion as of January 2022, an increase of $185 billion or close to 50%, compared to two years ago.

sections.label: NIRC average revenue stream
sections.summary: Over the past five years, the NIRC provided an average revenue stream of around $17 billion, or 3.5% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Over the past five years, the NIRC provided an average revenue stream of around $17 billion, or 3.5% of our GDP.

sections.label: GST raise during pandemic
sections.summary: Concern is raised about the risk of raising GST while the pandemic is ongoing and economic recovery has many uncertainties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: While economic growth seems to have started to pick up again, there are also some underlying concerns.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Hence, we are very concerned about the risk of raising GST when the pandemic is still ongoing and there are many uncertainties with the economic recovery.

sections.label: Corporate tax and global minimum
sections.summary: Singapore's effective corporate tax rate is close to 3%, below the OECD's announced global minimum tax rate of 15%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Our effective corporate tax rate is close to 3%, well below the global minimum tax rate of 15% announced by the OECD.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: If Singapore imposes a global minimum tax of 15% on MNCs subject to the tax reform, it will not only raise our corporate tax revenue significantly, but also achieve the objective of this Budget, which is to build a fairer and more resilient tax regime where people wealthier will contribute more.

sections.label: Customs duties and consumption taxes
sections.summary: In 1965 customs and excise duties were over 50% of tax revenue, now under 5%, and consumption taxes came only in 1994.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In Singapore, when we became a newly independent country in 1965, customs and excise duties made up more than 50% of the share of total tax revenue.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It steadily declined through the decades and now make up less than 5% of tax revenue.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Consumption taxes were introduced in Singapore only later in 1994.

sections.label: Budget 2022 top earners tax
sections.summary: Budget 2022 raises the marginal tax rate of the highest income earners, among other measures.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Budget 2022 raises the marginal tax rate of the highest income earners, among other measures.

sections.label: GST hike regressivity offset
sections.summary: Budget 2022 seeks to avoid the regressive nature of the consumption tax rate increase with the Assurance Package and by boosting permanent GST Vouchers.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Budget 2022 seeks to avoid the regressive nature of the increase in consumption tax rate with the Assurance Package and by boosting the permanent GST Vouchers (GSTV).

sections.label: Wage subsidies and supplements
